exercise1.prompt: Putting a Join to Work: Mean score per team, from two files

hiddenCases.name: different files give a different answer
pandas does the work
hiddenCases.describe: both files read and merged on id

exercise1.hint: Read both, merge on id, group by team, take the mean of score, round it, then to_dict(). The second file set is different, so a typed-in answer fails.

exercise2.prompt: Putting a Join to Work: Report the join, not just its result

hiddenCases.name: a duplicated key shows up as extra rows

exercise2.hint: Read both, left join, and report len(people), len(joined) and the count of NaN in the score column. A left join cannot lose rows, so more rows than people means a key was duplicated.

questions.prompt: When should the key checks happen?
questions.explain: Every one of them is cheap before and expensive after, once the totals are already wrong.

questions.prompt: A left join gives more rows than the left table had. What happened?
choices: The right table had a duplicated key
questions.explain: A left join cannot lose rows, so more rows than you started with means the right side multiplied them.

choices: A mean over multiplied rows looks entirely reasonable and is wrong
questions.explain: Nothing about the summary reveals that the table underneath it was the wrong one.

questions.prompt: What belongs beside a group mean in the report?
choices: The number of rows behind it
questions.explain: A team of one is not a comparison, and the reader cannot tell without the count.
